title: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza
text:
The Talmud says Jerusalem was destroyed because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza. A man in the city had a friend named Kamtza and an enemy named Bar Kamtza. He gave a feast and told his servant to invite Kamtza, but the servant brought Bar Kamtza instead.

When the host found his enemy at the table, he ordered him to leave. Bar Kamtza, mortified, offered to pay for whatever he ate if he could stay. The host refused. He offered to pay half the cost of the feast, then the whole of it. The host refused, took him by the hand and threw him out. Leading rabbis were among the guests, and none of them said a word.

Bar Kamtza decided that their silence meant they approved, and he went to the Roman emperor to accuse the Jews of rebellion. As proof, he said, send them a sacrifice and see if they will offer it. The emperor sent a fine calf, and on the way Bar Kamtza made a small cut in its lip, a blemish that disqualified it under Jewish law but not under Roman custom.

The rabbis debated offering it anyway for the sake of peace, or even killing Bar Kamtza, but Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas talked them out of both. The offering was refused, and in the Talmud's telling this set in motion the war that ended with the Temple in flames.
lesson: Humiliating someone in public, and staying silent while it happens, can set off consequences far beyond the moment. Speak up when you see someone shamed.
people: A host, Bar Kamtza, Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas, the rabbis
date: 1st century, as told in the Talmud
caveat: This is a rabbinic moral narrative, not a historical account of the causes of the Jewish War of 66 to 70 AD.
